content: Artificial respiration refers to the process of simulating breathing to facilitate the exchange of gases in the body, including pulmonary ventilation, external respiration, and internal respiration. This technique is used to provide air to individuals who are either not breathing or whose respiratory efforts are insufficient. However, it is essential that the patient has a beating heart, or artificial respiration must be performed as part of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) to enable internal respiration. Pulmonary ventilation, and by extension external respiration, is achieved by manually inflating the lungs. This can be done either by the rescuer blowing air directly into the patient’s lungs or by using a mechanical device. This method of insufflation has been shown to be more effective than older techniques involving mechanical manipulation of the patient’s chest or arms, such as the Silvester method. Artificial respiration is also referred to as Expired Air Resuscitation (EAR), Expired Air Ventilation (EAV), mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, or colloquially, the kiss of life. Artificial respiration is a critical component of most CPR protocols, making it an essential skill for first aid providers. In certain situations, such as near-drowning incidents or opiate overdoses, artificial respiration may be performed independently of full CPR. However, in most modern protocols, laypersons are advised to perform full CPR when a patient is not breathing adequately, while artificial respiration alone is typically reserved for healthcare professionals. Insufflations Insufflation, also known as rescue breaths or ventilations, involves mechanically forcing air into a patient’s respiratory system. This can be achieved through various methods, depending on the situation and available equipment. Effective airway management is crucial to ensure the success of any insufflation technique. Common methods include: Mouth-to-mouth: The rescuer forms a seal between their mouth and the patient’s mouth and blows air into the patient’s lungs. Mouth-to-nose: In cases such as maxillofacial injuries, water rescues, or when vomit is present in the patient’s mouth, the rescuer may form a seal with the patient’s nose instead. Mouth-to-mouth-and-nose: This method is typically used for infants (usually up to around one year old) as it provides the most effective seal. Mouth-to-mask: Many organizations recommend using a barrier device, such as a pocket mask, to reduce the risk of cross-infection. Pocket masks may also deliver higher tidal volumes than a bag-valve mask. Bag-valve mask (BVM): This manually operated device involves squeezing a bag to expel air into the patient’s lungs. Mechanical resuscitator: An electric device designed to provide automated breathing for the patient. Adjuncts to Insufflation To minimize the risk of cross-infection, most training organizations recommend using a protective barrier during any mouth-to-patient method. Examples of such barriers include pocket masks and keyring-sized face shields. These barriers are considered personal protective equipment (PPE) and protect the rescuer from exposure to potentially infectious materials, such as blood or vomit. They typically feature a one-way filter valve that allows air to flow from the rescuer to the patient while preventing substances from the patient from reaching the rescuer. Many adjuncts are single-use, but if they are reusable, they must be cleaned, autoclaved, and have their filters replaced after use. The CPR mask is the preferred method for ventilating a patient when only one rescuer is available. Many CPR masks include 18mm inlets to support supplemental oxygen, which increases the oxygen concentration delivered to the patient from approximately 17% (from the rescuer’s expired air) to around 40-50%. Tracheal intubation is often used for short-term mechanical ventilation. This involves inserting a tube through the nose (nasotracheal intubation) or mouth (orotracheal intubation) and advancing it into the trachea. Tubes with inflatable cuffs are commonly used to prevent leakage and aspiration. Intubation with a cuffed tube provides the best protection against aspiration. However, tracheal tubes can cause pain and coughing, so sedative drugs are usually administered unless the patient is unconscious or anesthetized. Other disadvantages of tracheal intubation include damage to the mucosal lining of the nasopharynx or oropharynx and the risk of subglottic stenosis. In emergencies, healthcare professionals may perform a cricothyrotomy, which involves creating a surgical opening in the cricothyroid membrane to insert an airway. This procedure is similar to a tracheostomy but is reserved for emergency access, such as when there is a complete blockage of the pharynx or severe maxillofacial injury that prevents the use of other adjuncts. Efficiency of Mouth-to-Patient Insufflation Normal atmospheric air contains approximately 21% oxygen. After gas exchange occurs in the lungs, the exhaled air typically contains around 17% oxygen, meaning the body utilizes only about 19% of the inhaled oxygen. This leaves over 80% of the oxygen available in the exhaled breath, which can be used to oxygenate the patient’s lungs and facilitate the formation of oxyhemoglobin. Oxygen The efficiency of artificial respiration can be significantly enhanced by combining it with oxygen therapy. The oxygen concentration delivered during mouth-to-mouth resuscitation is approximately 16%. When performed using a pocket mask with an oxygen flow, this increases to 40%. If a bag-valve mask or mechanical respirator is used with an oxygen supply, the concentration rises to 99%. Higher oxygen concentrations improve the efficiency of gas exchange in the lungs, making the process more effective.
